Brief Facts
2.

It is stated that on 12.08.2021, at about 06.31 pm, a sample of "Almonds" in sealed packs of 250 grams was lifted by Ms. Chittra Bamola, Food Safety Officer, for its analysis under the provisions of the Act from Sh. Mahesh Malik, FBO-cum- Partner (Appellant No.1) at M/s. Malik Brothers (Appellant No.3) from their outlet at 44, Defence Colony Market, New Delhi.
The sample was divided into four equal parts, fastened and sealed according to rules and regulations and signed by FBO and the same was sent to the Food Analyst, GNCTD for analysis on 13.08.2021.

The food Analyst analyzed the sample and reported the sample to be misbranded because there was violation of 2.2.1.7, 2.2.2.1, 2.2.2.4, 2.2.2.6, 2.2.2.7, 2.2.2.8, 2.2.2.9 & 2.2.2.10 of the Food Safety & Standards (Packaging & Labeling) Regulation, 2011.
Thereafter, the appellant was provided an opportunity to file an appeal u/s 46 (4) of FSS Act, however, no appeal was preferred by the appellants against the report of the Food Analyst.

Thereafter, Ld. Adjudicating Officer after going through the documents available on record found the appellant guilty for selling 'Misbranded Food Article' in violation of Section 23 (1), 26 (2) (ii), 27 (1), 27 (3) (c) read with Section 3 (1) (zf) of the FSS Act r/w Regulation No. 2.2.1.7, 2.2.2.1, 2.2.2.4, 2.2.2.6, 2.2.2.7, 2.2.2.8, 2.2.2.9 & 2.2.2.10 of the FSS (P & L) Regulation,
thereby imposing a penalty of Rs. 50,000/- each upon R-1 and R-2 and penalty of Rs. 1,00,000/-
upon R-3. GROUNDS OF APPEAL 3.
The appellants have assailed the impugned order passed by the Adjudicating Officer/Addl.

District Magistrate on the ground that it has been passed hurriedly without appreciating that the sampled commodity was not meant for sale to the consumers at large but were being packed as per customer's order.

It is further asserted that on analysis, the said sample was declared to be misbranded by the Food Analyst vide its report dated 26.08.2021 on the ground that the label of sample was without declaration of FSSAI Logo, Licence Number, name of food, vegetarian symbol,
name and complete address of manufacturer, net quantity, batch number, date of packing and best before date and, therefore, the sample contravened Sections 2.2.1.7, 2.2.2.1, 2.2.2.4, 2.2.2.6, 2.2.2.7,
2.2.2.8, 2.2.2.9 and 2.2.2.10 of the Food Safety & Standards (Packaging & Labeling) Regulation,
2011.

The sampled commodity was otherwise found conforming to the quality characteristics/parameters as prescribed under the Food Safety & Standards (Food Products Standards & Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, as reflected in Food Analyst's report dated 26.05.2021 ARGUMENTS Mahesh Malik And Others vs State Through Fso on 22 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/175803281/

sentences.text: I have heard the arguments of Sh. Satish Solanki and Ms. Samiksha, Ld. Counsels for the appellants and Sh. Vinod Kumar Sharma, Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor for the State/Respondent and have gone through the record of the Adjudicating Officer, record of the present appeal and documents filed therewith as well.

It is pertinent to mention here that the appellants had already accepted their guilt before the Adjudicating Authority thus, the scope of appeal becomes limited,
especially when it is not contended that the plea of guilt was not voluntary.

5. Notwithstanding the grounds of appeal taken, the counsel for the appellant has submitted, rather admitted, that the sampled product was to be labeled and stickers were to be pasted on the plastic packet but before it could be done, the sample was lifted.
It is further submitted that the Almonds were otherwise found to be conforming to the norms and requirements of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
Thus, in these circumstances, punishment awarded by the Adjudicating Officer/ADM is excessive, disproportionate and exorbitant.

6. The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and Regulations, 2011 are primarily, if not entirely,
concerned with the quality of the food and if it is found that it is free from adulteration of any nature, then the primary purpose of the food item stands achieved.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and Regulations, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The labeling and branding, etc are secondary aspect of the food safety measures.

In addition to the aforesaid contention, it has also been mentioned in the appeal that appellant No.3 is a partnership firm and Harish Malik was appointed Nominee under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, therefore, appellant No.1 Mahesh Malik was not responsible in any manner for the conduct of the business of appellant No.3.

Accordingly, there could not have been any punishment/penalty for appellant No.1.
7.

It is further asserted on behalf of the appellant that the request for taking a lenient view was,
apparently, declined by the Adjudicating Officer/ADM whereas the case of the appellant was a fit case where indulgence should have been given by the Adjudicating Authority in view of the fact that food product "Almonds" were free from any kind of adulteration, etc and conformed to the norms provided under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
The penalty imposed, it is submitted, is therefore arbitrary and harsh and is required to be waived off.
8. It is submitted that there is no independent witness for sampling and preparation of the documents related to the sampling which in itself is a ground to set aside the impugned order.

An opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses was not given to the appellant, therefore, the impugned order deserves to be set aside, through which the partnership firm, appellant No.3 and appellant No.1 and 2 i.e. Mahesh Malik and Harish Malik respectively have been imposed with a fine of Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lac only) on the partnership firm and Rs.50,000/- (Rupees Fifty Thousand only) each on the FBO, Nominee and the one found at the spot selling the 'Almonds'
respectively.
As referred earlier, the appellants have, since admitted their guilt, then the arguments on merit are not required to be considered.
The quantum of punishment is what can be looked into.

9. The Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor on behalf of the State/Respondent, on the other hand, contended that the requirements of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Regulations therein are required to be adhered to and there cannot be any pick and choose, as has been suggested by the appellant.

If misbranding is an offence, then in the case of misbranding, statutory punishment is Mahesh Malik And Others vs State Through Fso on 22 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/175803281/
3 required to be considered and awarded to the persons violating the laws, notwithstanding the fact that there was no flaw either in the quantity or quality of the product i.e. "Almond".

sentences.text:
As such, it is submitted that in the absence of any cogent reason, the impugned order is not required to be set aside.
10. Having taken into account the fact that the appellants had arranged the sample sticker which were to be pasted upon the packets of Almonds.
The contention that the appellant is selling his products in loose/open condition and in that situation, what was the occasion for the appellant to pack the Almonds in 250 grams of plastic pouches.

If it was made on order, as asserted by counsel for the appellant, then in order to establish its credentials, the appellants should have placed on record the order so received along with the sticker which were supposed to be pasted on the packets.

The absence of any such effort on the part of the appellants, gives reason to be believe that the appellants have not taken into account the facts which ought to have been taken into account and not acted in a manner in which they ought to have.
11. The other side of the coin is that the food item in question i.e. Almonds were conforming to the norms of quality as a food item.
The product was found upto the mark without there being any flaw or deficiency in any manner.

The object of the food related legislation is to ensure the quality of the food item and that the buyer is aware of the details of what is being purchased by him, which comes from the disclosures on the label/packaging, etc.

Again the inherent idea, in that too, is to ensure that quality and quantity of the food articles is maintained and that the address etc., of the manufacturer is there so as to fix the responsibility, if need be.

On these parameters of quality, the Almonds were found upto the mark and this opens a window for the appellants to be given some indulgence, which could have been extended by the Adjudicating Authority.

Thus, considering the entire gamut of facts and circumstances, the object of food related legislations, especially the fact that the food item was upto the mark, therefore, the penalty imposed upon the appellants is required to be mellowed down.

In a way, it can said that those sellers/dealers who are careful enough to maintain the quality of the food should be encouraged to maintain it and any action which may dampen the spirit should be avoided.
Thus, the penalty imposed upon the appellants is reduced to Rs.5,000/- each in respect of appellant Nos. 1 and 2 and in respect of appellant No.3 it is scaled down to the extent of Rs.10,000/- only.
With these observations, the appeal is partly allowed and accordingly stands disposed off.
A copy of this order with the record of the Adjudicating Authority be sent back.
12. File be consigned to Record Room.
